title: A Latin American Fable
subtitle: A salute to a literary society born within a prison—no, a tribute to an impossible miracle.

content.text: Let's take a step back—pull you out of that whirlwind of passion and dreams.
If you want to make the best call, you need to zero in on what really matters. So, what's your take on that big speech?

branch.text: A sudden explosion that shook Latin American literary circles about 30 years ago. It was destructive—but also gave rise to new life.
Lucky for us, we don't have to worry about shell shock in the literary world.

content.text: You don't strike me as someone who knows about literature.

branch.text: It's not about knowing literature. Any soldier with a little experience can deliver a status report. Alright, eyes on the map.
As we speak, ships are lined up on the Spanish coast—but this time, they're poised to make a new kind of discovery, if you can call it that.
And here are our new "Columbuses," heading to the docks to embark on their journey.
Carmen and Carlos, the driving force behind this literary feast between Spain and Latin America.
Carmen, with an eye for opportunity and a mind for business, sought out the continent's literary gems and secured generous publishing deals for them.
Carlos, with his deep understanding of market dynamics, brought these works to the eyes of the European public.
Then? A golden era began. It all kicked off with a scandal at a military academy, and soon the entire world was captivated by the story of a baby with a pig's tail from a faraway land.
But we mustn't forget the writers themselves. Fuentes, a towering figure of the Spanish-speaking world, and Cortázar, the writer ever seeing through the eyes of a child.
And of course, Mario and Gabo—key players in this literary revolution—will forever be etched in the annals of history.
They corresponded regularly, always expressing deep admiration for each other's work. In fact, one even wrote a doctoral thesis on the other.
Ah, friendship.

content.text: That must have been a proud time for them.

branch.text: It was.
But no matter how explosive the boom was, it couldn't escape its fleeting nature.
With the second imprisonment and self-criticism of a Cuban poet, in came an inexplicable right hook, and bang!—silence.
The military junta had gripped the poets' throats. The verse of the pioneers was cut off, their voices no longer heard.
The bond between two generations was broken, and for the younger of the two, the silence was intolerable.
They looked for a new theme, a new idea, a new voice—a new method to speak on their disappointment, their horror, and their anger.
And they became the new guerrillas.

trails.title: The Weaving of Shadows, Volume II
trails.description: Towering walls, prisoners deep in the abyss paint pictures of the sky.

items.text: A Latin American Fable
Hall of New Encounters

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: I didn't expect any of this from what we saw outside.
The mottled yet pristine walls, the still waters, the silent white tower standing within the labyrinth.
Nearby, several prisoners form a circle, some standing, some sitting, engaged in conversation.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: *sigh* Excuse me for a moment. I have duties that I must attend to.
With a sigh, the jailer steps into the gathering, causing a strangely subdued reaction from the prisoners.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: They don't seem intimidated by her at all.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Yeah, they just look like a bunch of artists having a chat in the garden. And the jailer seems to be like a grumpy neighbor coming over to ask them to keep it down.
The "grumpy neighbor" continues her chastising.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Everyone, you know the rules. There are to be no after-hours gatherings here without the Physician's approval.

items.speaker: Inmate I
items.text: You sound softer and softer each time you come to warn us. Why not just join us? Isn't it better than circling around the Panopticon all day?

items.speaker: Inmate I
items.text: And look around you. We're in the Hall of New Encounters. What better place to host a salon?

items.speaker: Inmate II
items.text: You're missing out in Comala if you don't even get a taste of our literature.

items.speaker: Inmate I
items.text: Exactly. Even those oil-dripping musicians drop by from time to time. Not that they're the kind to care about the beauty of words.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: Oil-dripping musicians? Timekeeper, could they mean—
Before the jailer can say anything else, two of the prisoners simultaneously gesture for her to stay silent, pointing to the center of their gathering.

items.speaker: Inmate I
items.text: Quiet now, please! The Idealist's salon is about to start.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: These people seem friendly enough. Why don't we see what this is about?

items.speaker: Gathering Participant I
items.text: In deserts, in stars, within labyrinths,

items.speaker: Gathering Participant II
items.text: In waters, in mirrors, within reflections,

items.speaker: Gathering Participant III
items.text: We dream on death's straw pillow.

items.speaker: Gathering Participant IV
items.text: Here we are, paying tribute to the ghosts,

items.speaker: Gathering Participant V
items.text: To give it all up again.

items.speaker: All Participants
items.text: To give it all up again.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: My dear friends, we face a difficult truth: the movement of visceral realism still stumbles in the dark.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Our poems, our language, our minds are tangled by a stifling vine—a mundane, stale vision shared among all bourgeoisie.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: We follow this vision blindly, clinging to the comfort brought by logic and conventional wisdom, and by it, we nip every branch of new art in the bud.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Poems are perhaps too fragile an outgrowth to develop one's life upon. But here, we may light them like candles at our funerals.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Let poetry become the bridge between us and the world.
A lone clap breaks the silence. It comes earlier than all the other cheers from the audience.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: As we come back and forth over the boundaries of life and death, the old obstacles begin to take on a new look. With the eyes of poets, we may see behind them.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: You're a visceral realist.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: I can't be mistaken. You must be—
The Idealist's eyes pierce through the grove of literary enthusiasts, reaching a distant, drifting new world.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: A lonely cowboy. Finally home.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: What a wonder.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: You're in time. The salon has just begun. And La Sociedad de Poetas de las Américas isn't like those salons that care more about who's invited than the art. All are welcome here.

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: A literary salon in a prison? Though so far it seems to have more dancing than poems.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Did you understand what that man just said?

items.speaker: Sonetto
items.text: No, sorry, Timekeeper. I need a moment to think it through.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Don't worry, Sonetto. I would guess we're not the only ones who are confused here.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Ms. Jailer, is this that peculiarity about Comala you mentioned earlier?

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Enough, Idealist. You're still an inmate here, and you're walking a very fine line right now.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Oh, I'm quite aware of where I am and what lines I tread.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: This is a prison. The safest place for poets in this part of the continent. One cannot be arrested twice, after all.
The man's words draw laughter from the other prisoners as they turn to discuss the speech with excitement.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: But please, don't trouble yourself with our little farce. What harm could a few poets possibly do?
All the irregular rhymes and wild contradictions of aesthetics converge into a chaotic countercurrent, crashing against the newcomers.
Recoleta clenches her fists in shock—certain that the man before her is her mysterious pen pal.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Mr. Idealist? Might I ask you something?

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Hold on, Recoleta. All forms of communication with the inmates must conform to our regulations. We will need to record the conversation and submit it to higher authorities for review.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I have some questions for the gentleman as well, but we're more than willing to follow the rules.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I think the person I'm looking for might have attended this literary salon, or at least talked to some of its members.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: I'd wager she's spoken to that gentleman. That is ... if she has been here at all.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I see. Go ahead then. Just watch the time.
As the visitors petition the jailer, Recoleta pushes past the bustling crowd and takes a deep breath.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: *deep breath* Are you Aleph?
The noisy atmosphere plunges into silence, just like the still waters nearby.
The Idealist is evidently taken aback by the name.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Oh! *chuckle* Another visitor looking for Aleph.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: So you know him!

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Naturally. But I'm not obliged to speak of him to one who does not, stranger.
The salon host is noncommittal, turning toward Recoleta's companions.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: And you, young lady in the hat? Are you here for Aleph as well? What a lively day this is!

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: No. I'm looking for a blind woman. Her name is Dores.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Ah, yes. I remember. Her writing was impeccable, like an exquisite crocodile-skin handbag in a shop window, elegant, yet condescending.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: Do you know where she is now?

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: I'm not able to keep track of every inmate here, Miss.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Perhaps you should ask those who have seen everything from above.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Through the glass, where the scrutinizing eyes of power look down on us.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: Eyes?
She scans the prison hall. The walls, the great tower, and the pool remain unchanged. Nothing appears amiss.
All the prisoners present nod in agreement, prompting a weary sigh from the jailer.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Have you taken your medicine today, Idealist?

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: I'm feeling marvelous! Today, I require no help from them!

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I've warned you. It's unwise to act against the Physician's orders.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Act against him? No one may act against him here.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: The Physician must have misunderstood us. I suspect he doesn't understand half of what we say. I'd like to know how he got his medical degree. Not by cracking open skulls, I should hope.
The prisoners exchange knowing smiles.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: What a pity, Jailer! You know, I've always believed you had the soul of a poet, just like us.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text:
We've already spoken enough "rebellious thoughts" outside of Comala. 
How else do you think we ended up in your nuthouse?

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: We've been here far too long, long after the Junta was removed from office,

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: after our home became a deserted wasteland in the aftermath of the Latin American Boom.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: What are you getting at?

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: That power is boring, meaningless. Nothing holds onto power forever.

items.speaker: Recoleta
items.text: And the one true connection we have to life is poetry.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: See, Jailer? Even an outsider understands our ideas better than you. It's time to open your eyes to reality.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: La Sociedad is the only way for us to feel truly alive in here, beneath the gaze of those prying, ever-vigilant eyes.

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: Idealist! Last warning. Stop this now.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Fine, fine! Alright, companions. Sadly, the salon must come to an end, as our jailer insists.
The crowd murmurs and grumbles as they begin to disperse.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Dear friends, I do not mean to abuse the power of suspense. I sincerely invite you to come with me to the heart of La Sociedad de Poetas de las Américas.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Perhaps you'll find the person you look for there.
The man strikes a gesture somehow equally comedic and solemn.

items.speaker: Vertin
items.text: We'd love to. Umm, only if that's okay with you, Ms. Jailer?

items.speaker: Jailer
items.text: I suppose that's alright. You're already here; we can call it part of your tour. But, please, ladies, take none of their ramblings seriously.

items.speaker: The Idealist
items.text: Thank you, Jailer! Please, follow me.
